items.title: Disk winds from T Tauri stars - physics and observables
items.abstract: Magnetically driven disk winds are fundamental to protoplanetary disk evolution, regulating angular momentum transport, stellar accretion, disk dispersal, and the environment in which planets form. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) models provide the theoretical framework for understanding how large-scale magnetic fields launch, accelerate, and collimate these outflows, while establishing direct links between the underlying physics and observable diagnostics. This review presents an overview of analytical magnetized disk-wind models developed primarily for T Tauri stars. We summarize the physical foundations of magnetized outflows, from early magnetized wind theories to self-consistent accretion–ejection solutions, emphasizing the roles of magnetic geometry, angular momentum extraction, magnetic lever arms, mass loading, and non-ideal MHD effects in determining wind structure and efficiency. We review the observational diagnostics predicted by analytical models, including spectroscopic, kinematic, thermo-chemical, and molecular signatures that constrain the wind-launching region, acceleration, collimation, and angular momentum transport. We also briefly discuss how modern numerical simulations extend analytical theory by incorporating non-ideal MHD, realistic thermodynamics, radiative transfer, chemistry, dust evolution, and time-dependent processes that cannot be treated self-consistently within the assumptions of analytical models. By linking MHD theory, analytical solutions, observations, and numerical simulations, this review emphasizes the enduring importance of analytical disk-wind models as the conceptual framework for interpreting magnetized outflows from protoplanetary disks and their role in the evolution of young planetary systems.

items.title: Regimes of truth in postmodern novels: the atlas of misty continents in the context of modernity and Ottoman epistemology
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the epistemological transformation concerning the nature and legitimacy of knowledge in the context of modernity and postmodernity through İhsan Oktay Anar’s The Atlas of Misty Continents. While modernity conceptualizes knowledge as a universal structure grounded in reason and empirical verification, postmodern thought challenges these assumptions by arguing that knowledge is produced within historical, cultural, and discursive processes. Accordingly, truth is not treated as a fixed entity but rather as a contextual and pluralized construction. The study examines the core concepts of postmodern epistemology through Jean-François Lyotard’s critique of “grand narratives” and his notion of “language games,” as well as Michel Foucault’s framework of the knowledge–power relationship. Although these perspectives do not entirely deny the possibility of objective reality, they emphasize that knowledge gains legitimacy through specific discursive and institutional formations. By extending this theoretical framework into the field of literature, the article discusses how the postmodern novel represents regimes of knowledge. In this respect, it argues that in The Atlas of Misty Continents, knowledge is constructed in multiple forms, drawing not only on scientific rationality but also on sources such as rumor, intuition, tradition, and dreams. The novel is analyzed through categories including narrative reliability, the representation of knowledge sources, the pluralization of truth claims, and the distribution of epistemic authority. The study contends that Anar does not merely juxtapose modern and postmodern epistemologies but instead incorporates them simultaneously and equivalently within fiction. Consequently, this article argues that The Atlas of Misty Continents is not merely an aesthetic work of fiction; rather, it constructs a mode of thinking that simultaneously draws on postmodern epistemology and the Ottoman epistemic framework.

items.title: WALLABY pilot survey: accurate and automated linewidth measurements from global H i profiles
items.abstract: Abstract Current-generation 21-cm surveys of extragalactic neutral hydrogen (H i) with instruments such as FAST and ASKAP are providing detailed spectral and spatial information for over 105 galaxies. Future H i surveys with next-generation radio telescopes could provide sample sizes larger by orders of magnitude. There is therefore a need for accurate, automated, and reliable parameterisation of the H i emission from galaxies. We have developed an automated estimator for H i global profile widths to better enable studies of, for example, dynamical masses and Tully-Fisher distances. Our estimator is based on an implementation of the BusyFit profile-fitting algorithm, and converges for 95 % of global profiles in the WALLABY pilot survey. Probability density functions are calculated for all profile parameters using Monte Carlo techniques, and example error parameterisations are given. We confirm that linewidth uncertainties depend primarily on the integrated signal-to-noise ratio, profile steepness, and the linewidth, consistent with previous studies. We compare several common linewidth definitions, and the width at 50 % of the mean flux density (Wm50) is found to be the most robust measure of linewidth. We provide examples of the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation drawn from the WALLABY pilot survey.

items.title: Classification of chiral domain-wall dynamics through symmetry analysis
items.abstract: We report the discovery of a previously unreported type of chiral domain-wall (DW) dynamics and establish a symmetry-based framework for classifying the observed types of chiral DW dynamics. In this newly identified type, the symmetric component of the DW speed exhibits a concave-down curvature, in sharp contrast to the conventional concave-up response associated with the equilibrium DW-energy contribution. Sample-specific micromagnetic calculations reproduce only the conventional response and fail to account for this reversed curvature, indicating an additional even contribution beyond the conventional equilibrium DW-energy picture. By incorporating this new response, we show that the chiral DW dynamics observed to date can be classified into three distinct types, all of which are quantitatively described by symmetric and antisymmetric components having the same respective functional forms. This classification provides a systematic framework for investigating diverse chiral DW dynamics and their underlying physics.

items.title: A 13CO Detection in a Massive Molecular Gas Flow in Abell 1795’s Central Galaxy
items.abstract: Abstract We present new ALMA 13CO(2-1) observations of the central galaxy in the cool-core cluster Abell 1795, targeting the origin of extended molecular filaments. The filaments extend for 5–7 kpc and are closely drawn up around large radio bubbles inflated by jets from the central active galactic nucleus (AGN). Smooth velocity gradients along their lengths are consistent with entrained flows lifted by the expanding bubbles. Here we detect the northern molecular filament in the low-opacity molecular tracer 13CO(2-1) , which can provide a more reliable measure of the molecular gas mass and conditions than 12CO . The velocity structure in 13CO(2-1) is consistent with that of the 12CO (2-1) emission. Using a range of plausible excitation temperatures and covering fractions, we thereby determine a filament molecular gas mass of (0.1–2) × 109 M⊙, or down to an order of magnitude below previous estimates. This implies a CO-to-H2 conversion factor of αCO = 0.4–5 M⊙ (K km s−1 pc2)−1 in the filament, or ∼ 0.1–1 times the standard assumption of the Milky Way value. Direct entrainment by the N radio bubble is now plausible, as it can provide sufficient mechanical energy and buoyant support for the molecular gas flow. Similarly, measured X-ray cooling rates are also now consistent with in-situ condensation of uplifted, low-entropy hot gas. Both formation mechanisms require multiple generations of bubbles at higher filament masses.

items.title: Conditional Derivative GANs for Parameter-Conditioned Synthesis of Gravitational Waves from Core-Collapse Supernovae
items.abstract: Abstract Gravitational wave signals from core-collapse supernovae encode critical astrophysical information, including key astrophysical parameters such as the ratio of rotational kinetic to gravitational potential energy at bounce, pre-collapse differential rotation, and the nuclear equation of state. However, the limited number of observed core-collapse supernovae events makes it challenging to build robust data-driven models. The generation of synthetic gravitational wave signals from core-collapse supernovae can therefore provide a valuable tool for data augmentation in machine learning pipelines, particularly for the training and testing of detection and parameter estimation algorithms. Although recent efforts have explored the use of generative models to synthesize waveform-like data, existing approaches lack the ability to condition outputs on specific astrophysical parameters. To address this, we propose a model capable of generating gravitational wave signals conditioned on astrophysical parameters of core-collapse supernovae rotation. The proposed conditional derivative generative adversarial network is trained on the Richers et al. catalog, which contains 1,824 simulated time-series gravitational wave waveforms and their corresponding physical parameters. Quantitative evaluation using time-domain similarity and distributional metrics shows that the generated signals reproduce the key statistical and morphological features of the original dataset. This work introduces a conditional generative framework for rotating core-collapse supernovae gravitational wave signals, that enables fast, low-cost data augmentation and parameterized modeling, improving ML-based detection and parameter estimation.

items.title: DIGITAL ELECTORAL RECAPITULATION SYSTEMS AND GOVERNANCE MODELS: COMPARATIVE INTERNATIONAL EVIDENCE
items.abstract: This study compares the management of election recapitulation information systems in Indonesia with those implemented in the Philippines, Brazil, Estonia, and Kyrgyzstan to examine differences in governance, system design, security mechanisms, digital infrastructure, transparency, and public trust. Although these countries have adopted various election technologies, ranging from optical scanning and Electronic Voting Machines (EVM) to Internet voting (i-voting) and optical tabulation, comprehensive comparative studies that position Indonesia within this international context remain limited. This study employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Data were collected from the Scopus database and supported by credible reports, while CiteSpace was used to map research trends and identify knowledge gaps. The findings reveal significant differences in the maturity of election recapitulation systems. Estonia and Brazil have achieved advanced digital election management through integrated digital governance, secure verification mechanisms, and high public trust. The Philippines applies a hybrid model combining paper ballots with automated vote counting, whereas Kyrgyzstan continues to rely largely on manual procedures. Indonesia's Sirekap represents an intermediate stage of digital transformation but continues to face challenges related to security, OCR accuracy, infrastructure readiness, and public trust. The theoretical contribution of this study is the development of a Comparative Governance Framework for Election Recapitulation Information Systems, demonstrating that system maturity is determined not only by technological adoption but also by the interaction among governance, security, digital infrastructure, transparency, and public trust. This framework provides a foundation for evaluating and improving election recapitulation systems in emerging digital democracies.

items.title: «¡Que no entre aquí ningún ignorante en Geometría!» ¿Quién dibujó los patrones geométricos meriníes?
items.abstract: Los intrincados patrones de zillīǧ en las madāris meriníes de Fez —especialmente en al-ʿAṭṭārīn y Bū ʿInānīya— problematizan la intersección entre la geometría teórica y la práctica artesanal en su diseño, así como su agencia y contexto cultural. Esta investigación cuestiona la autoría de estos patrones, argumentando que su sofisticación trasciende los métodos artesanales tradicionales y refleja, en cambio, el conocimiento erudito auspiciado por el mecenazgo meriní. Mediante el análisis de la brecha epistémica entre la geometría teórica (como la articularon polímatas como al-Kindī, al-Fārābī e Ibn Ḫaldūn) y las técnicas prácticas de los artesanos (documentadas en cuadernos de bocetos y manuales), el artículo demuestra que los diseños decagonales e icosagonales de los zillīǧ meriní requerían una precisión euclidiana incompatible con las técnicas de las tradiciones artesanales. Las construcciones pentagonales y decagonales en estas madāris —notablemente ausentes en los manuales de artesanía tradicional existentes— sugieren la participación directa de las élites intelectuales, posiblemente polímatas como Ibn al-Bannāʾ al-Marrākušī. Al contextualizar estos patrones dentro de las estrategias de legitimación de la dinastía meriní, el estudio revela cómo la ornamentación geométrica funcionó tanto como una declaración intelectual como una herramienta política, reforzando la autoridad dinástica a través del mecenazgo cultural y científico. El artículo concluye que estos diseños fueron creados para un público instruido en geometría, incorporando significados accesibles solo para la élite erudita, en consonancia con el aforismo de la Academia Platónica: «Que ningún ignorante en geometría entre aquí». Por lo tanto, para un análisis correcto de los patrones geométricos islámicos, los historiadores del arte deben examinar tanto las construcciones matemáticas euclidianas como su contexto cultural de producción.

items.title: False Dawn (Fajar Kāżib) in Hadith and Islamic Astronomy
items.abstract: False dawn (fajar kāżib) is a pre-dawn luminous phenomenon significant in hadith, Islamic jurisprudence, and Islamic astronomy. Hadith describe it as vertically rising light resembling a wolf’s tail that neither marks the beginning of the Subuh prayer time nor signals the end of the pre-dawn meal. This study examines the interpretation of hadith descriptions of false dawn by integrating normative hadith narratives, juristic explanations, and published astronomical evidence. It employs a qualitative-interdisciplinary approach combining textual analysis, juristic interpretation, and documented astronomical observations. The observational materials include field images, sky-brightness data measured using a Sky Quality Meter (SQM), Stellarium-based visual comparisons, and sky-condition analyses from Bayan, North Lombok, recorded on 7–8 October 2024. The analysis proceeds through three stages: interpreting the hadith descriptions, examining their juristic implications, and comparing the visual characteristics of false dawn with astronomical explanations of zodiacal light. The findings suggest that false dawn can be understood phenomenologically as dim, vertically extending, non-horizontal light appearing before true dawn (fajar ṣādiq). These characteristics resemble zodiacal light, which results from sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust concentrated around the ecliptic plane. This synthesis demonstrates that hadith provides visual indicators and legal boundaries, while Islamic astronomy offers a physical explanation grounded in existing scientific literature. The study concludes that integrating hadith interpretation with astronomical evidence can strengthen scientific and Sharīʿah-based understanding of false dawn without altering the normative role of hadith in determining prayer times.

items.title: Spaceflight-associated Motion Sickness in Commercial Crew Astronauts
items.abstract: Spaceflight-associated motion sickness, including space motion sickness (SMS) and terrestrial readaptation motion sickness (TRMS), has presented as the most operationally limiting effect on the human in the days following a gravity transition. Published data suggest that astronaut head movements provoke symptoms, but those studies rarely controlled for them. Most previous studies use postflight retrospective reporting and have not quantified temporal dynamics or persistence of symptoms; no study has published motion sickness in a cohort of commercial flyers. Here, we comprehensively evaluate SMS and TRMS within commercial flyers (N=8; 4F, 4M) for the first time, across two commercial missions of short duration (Polaris Dawn and Fram2). Utilizing a standard reporting methodology, we find an 87.5% incidence of SMS, which persisted for at least three days on orbit in 25% of crewmembers. The symptoms included vomiting in 62.5% of crewmembers. Regarding TRMS, incidence was 50%, severity was significantly lower than SMS (p = 0.007), and it tended to persist for a shorter duration than SMS for these short-duration flights. These findings establish a systematic baseline for spaceflight-associated motion sickness, informing its operational impact and salience as human spaceflight missions expand in accessibility and scope.

items.title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
items.abstract: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.

items.title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
items.abstract: Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.

items.title: Fundamental Bounds on the Oscillation Efficiency of Markov Networks
items.abstract: Stochastic oscillations are commonly identified through peaks in their power spectra, yet the fundamental limits on their strength and energetic cost remain unclear. Here we establish universal dynamical and thermodynamic bounds on oscillation efficiency in Markov networks, showing how finite state spaces constrain spectral peak enhancement. In particular, we demonstrate that networks maximizing modal coherence need not maximize oscillation efficiency. We further derive dissipation bounds that connect oscillation efficiency to the relaxation speed and stationary probabilities, revealing an unavoidable energetic cost of maintaining pronounced oscillations at a specified relaxation timescale. These bounds remain strictly positive in regimes where existing explicit spectral dissipation estimates vanish, with stronger constraints for normal networks and uniform rings. Our results distinguish spectral oscillatory strength from modal coherence and reveal how network dynamics and thermodynamic dissipation jointly limit stochastic oscillations.

items.title: EEG Lempel-Ziv Complexity vis-à-vis Autocorrelation Function
items.abstract: Measures of signal complexity have become increasingly popular in electroencephalography (EEG), where they are often interpreted as indicators of neural information processing, dynamical richness, or conscious state. In contrast, classical measures of temporal dependence, such as the autocorrelation function (ACF), remain more directly linked to known physiological mechanisms and are easier to interpret. The present work revisits, for the EEG practicioner, the relation between normalized Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC) and temporal autocorrelation in both synthetic and physiological EEG signals. First, synthetic time series exhibiting a broad range of temporal structure and complexity levels were generated using stochastic processes with varying degrees of temporal dependence. LZC and autocorrelation measures were then computed and compared. Across simulated signals, a robust inverse relationship was observed between normalized LZC and the first autocorrelation coefficient, indicating that signals with stronger temporal correlations exhibit lower complexity estimates. This relationship also holds in resting-state EEG recordings from healthy adult participants across channels and subjects, as well as dynamically during eyes open/close maneuvers. Overall, these results show that the information captured by LZC reflects temporal redundancy already quantified by conventional autocorrelation measures. Because autocorrelation measures relate more directly to established neurophysiological mechanisms, including oscillatory persistence, network synchronization, and temporal integration, these results suggest that interpreting complexity-based EEG findings should explicitly account for their dependence on conventional temporal statistics, which may provide a more transparent framework for mechanistic inferences.

items.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
items.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.

items.title: The wealth-to-salary ratio: a simple indicator of inequality
items.abstract: In previous studies, using agent-based simulations of a model of a capitalist economy proposed by Ian Wright, we showed that inequality in both wealth and income distributions is largely governed by a single key parameter: the ratio between average wealth per capita and the mean salary, denoted by $R$. This parameter captures the relative importance of accumulated assets compared with labor income. In the model, larger values of $R$ are systematically associated with higher levels of inequality, as measured by the Gini coefficient. In the present work, we investigate whether this relationship is also observed in real-world economies. Using empirical data from the World Inequality Database (WID) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), we construct empirical estimates of $R$ and compare them with standard measures of income and wealth inequality. We find a positive relation between $R$ and inequality across several empirical settings, with the strongest relationships observed for mature and advanced economies. These results provide empirical support for the role of the wealth-to-salary ratio as a simple macroscopic indicator associated with economic inequality, while also highlighting the limitations imposed by differences in data definitions and measurement across countries and periods.

items.title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
items.abstract: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.

items.title: Microbial Methanogenesis on Mars: A Life Detection Target for an MLE-Type Mission and Future Human Exploration
items.abstract: Methane (CH4) is one of the most enigmatic and potentially consequential trace gases detected on Mars, having demonstrated apparent seasonality, localized plumes, or, depending on who you ask, never conclusively detected at all. While the Martian methane mystery remains unsolved, it has sparked a vibrant area of astrobiology research exploring whether microbial methanogenesis -- one of the simplest and most ancient metabolic pathways -- could plausibly proceed under various extreme physicochemical conditions characteristic of the Martian shallow subsurface. The emerging consensus is a cautious but compelling "possibly". These findings elevate methanogenesis as both a top priority candidate biosignature for extant life detection and a justification for urgently advancing in situ instrumentation capable of definitively detecting CH4 and constraining its origin, biotic or otherwise

items.title: Entering the Era of Circumplanetary Ring Detection with Direct Imaging
items.abstract: Rings are ubiquitous among the giant planets in the Solar System, yet their presence around exoplanets remains observationally unconstrained. As direct imaging missions such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope approach first light, understanding the influence of circumplanetary rings on reflected light photometry is critical for the accurate interpretation and follow-up of direct imaging observations. We present a hybrid forward model for reflected light phase curves of ringed exoplanets, coupling a ray casting framework for computing mutual planet-ring shadowing with empirical reflectance spectra from Cassini observations of Saturn's rings. We model Jupiter-like planets with opaque, icy rings spanning 1 - 10x the radial extent of Saturn's A, B, and C rings across a grid of inclinations and ring obliquities. Our simulations show that rings enhance the flux ratios at favorable ring geometries. Saturn-equivalent rings increase peak flux by a factor of 3.1 in the visible, while more extended rings produce enhanced contrasts exceeding an order of magnitude more. The flux contribution of a ring is highly sensitive to obliquity and orbital location. At certain geometries, rings can suppress total system brightness below that of a ringless planet. We highlight multi-band observations as a complementary route for diagnosing the presence of an exoring. We also apply the model to $\upsilon$ Andromedae d as an observational test case and discuss the implications for exoring detectability with the Roman Coronagraph. Exorings have the potential to bias inferred planetary properties from direct images and must be properly accounted for in observation preparation and interpretation.

items.title: Detecting Exoplanetary Rings with Roman CGI Reflected Light Phase Curve Observations
items.abstract: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) will provide the first opportunity to directly detect mature giant exoplanets in reflected light. However, most known radial-velocity planets lie near CGI's sensitivity limit. In contrast, Saturn-like rings around these planets may be much more accessible: our models show that rings can outshine their host planets by one to two orders of magnitude or more, making them easier to detect than the planets themselves. However, because the planet and rings would be unresolved in reflected light, unrecognized rings could lead to misinterpretation of the planet's intrinsic brightness and physical properties. To disentangle these blended signals, we model reflected-light phase curves of ringed and ringless planets. Ring systems can produce a distinctive phase-curve morphology, often with four extrema rather than the two expected for unringed planets, enabling robust confirmation with multi-epoch CGI observations. We develop an analytical framework for ringed-planet phase curves using a modern, self-consistent coordinate system and use it to illustrate phase curves for a range of ring configurations. We then simulate observations of $ε$ Eridani b (3.5 AU, 1 M$_{Jup}$), a prime initial CGI target, with a Saturn-like ring system. These simulations show that such a configuration would be detectable and suggest that rings may expand the pool of viable CGI targets to planets previously considered beyond reach. We conclude that CGI is poised to provide the first observational constraints on the prevalence of Saturn-like rings around giant exoplanets.

items.title: Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
items.abstract: Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

items.title: Two Seconds per Day: Limitations of Circadian Burden Metrics in the Permanent Daylight Saving Time Debate
items.abstract: A 1410-word Letter to the Editor reporting a bug in a study published in PNAS. The authors of the original study executed their code to compute the yearly circadian burden with an Earth rotating backwards: the sun rising in the West, setting on the East. The authors have acknowledged the error and re-executed the code. We analyze authors's new average yearly circadian burden in the US to show that these results do not provide significant information for the current debate on the time policy.

items.title: Survey of Orion Disks with ALMA (SODA) IV: Millimeter variability of protoplanetary disks
items.abstract: Context. Short-term millimeter-wavelength variability in Class II young stellar objects (YSOs) has been considered minimal, often dismissed as very rare in ALMA-based studies on short timescales. However, recent findings suggest that variability on sub-day timescales is significant. Aims. This study aims to quantify short timescale (~1 hour to ~3 days) millimeter flux variability in unresolved Class II YSO disks observed as part of the SODA survey, leveraging its large dataset to assess the statistical significance of such variability across the LDN 1641 and LDN 1647 regions in Orion. Methods. We analyze ALMA Band 6 observations of 873 YSOs obtained over multiple epochs using a custom flux extraction pipeline to separate individual execution blocks. By computing variability factors and statistical deviations from the mean flux, we identify sources exhibiting significant variability, accounting for noise and calibrator stability. Results. Even with conservative selection criteria, we identify 20 variable sources within the sample (~5.3% of all detections). The maximum of the measured variability factor is >=7 over about one hour. More liberal selection criteria yield up to 60 sources that could be called potentially variable (~15.9%). Conclusions. The number of variable sources detected in our sample indicates physical processes operating on time scales of hours, likely associated with magnetic reconnection and/or synchrotron radiation or strong cases of magnetic accretion changes. These detections show the need to reconsider typical stability assumptions in single-epoch observations and calls for follow-up studies in star-forming regions with ALMA. Masses derived from unresolved measurements could potentially be biased by this sort of variability.

items.title: A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster
items.abstract: We present a comprehensive spectroscopic census of the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC), based primarily on low-resolution optical spectroscopy obtained with MMT/Hectospec. We derive spectral types, youth indicators, and accretion diagnostics for 1513 stars located in the ONC region, enabling the identification and characterization of pre-main-sequence stars. We combine these measurements with a kinematic membership analysis based on Gaia Data Release 3 astrometry to identify and confirm cluster members. Using these combined diagnostics, we identify and characterize 780 bona fide T Tauri stars associated with the ONC. In addition, we construct a census of protoplanetary discs using infrared photometry obtained with the IRAC and MIPS instruments aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. We further derive stellar masses, ages, and extinctions using the MassAge code, which combines photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models, and employs a Monte Carlo approach for uncertainty propagation. The resulting homogeneous catalogue of ONC members provides spectroscopic characterizations, kinematic membership constraints, disc diagnostics, and self-consistent estimates of stellar physical parameters. This dataset offers a refined view of the stellar population of the ONC and provides a robust foundation for investigating its kinematic structure, age distribution, and protoplanetary disc population.

items.title: The Atmospheric Chemistry and Surface Interactions on Mars (ACSIOM) Workshop 2025
items.abstract: The ACSIOM workshop was held in Cambridge from 10th-12th November 2025. Its primary aims were twofold: 1) to gather UK researchers involved in Mars atmospheric science to identify current shortcomings and challenges in the field, and 2) to discuss possible collaborations and future steps needed to maximise the research output from current and future Mars missions. Workshop attendees spanned a wide range of subjects and disciplines, from atmospheric modellers and surface scientists to experimental chemists and Earth/Venus/exoplanet scientists. One of the primary outcomes of the workshop as identified by the attendees was the need for more collaborations between these different communities. It was agreed that we currently lack sufficient interaction between disciplines and this is a key challenge we need to overcome in order to properly utilise and exploit the vast pool of martian expertise available in the UK. Modellers need reaction rates from experimentalists; experimentalists need modelling context to prioritise their experiments; geologists need modelling context to understand the features they see; modellers need geological context to constrain their results. Attendees stressed that the UK Mars community has a critical mass which is internationally recognised, and improving the communication between communities would allow significant progress to be made in martian research, allowing the UK to maintain leadership in Mars science for years to come. We highlight that this is a pivotal moment for such investments as many planetary missions, both for Mars and other terrestrial bodies, are about to be launched or are being considered in the coming years. Having a strong and close-knit community will be key to better identifying needs and capabilities in order to optimise investments in missions and to have the best scientific return possible.

items.title: Stationary analysis of adaptive aspiration dynamics in graph-structured games
items.abstract: Aspiration dynamics can favor cooperation on finite graphs through a purely local satisfaction mechanism. In the model studied here, individuals compare their payoffs with adaptive aspiration levels and revise their strategies through a self-switching Fermi rule. Although the aspirations are continuous and endogenous, the resulting finite-population process has a unique stationary distribution for every finite selection intensity and every finite connected graph under degree-normalized average payoffs when restricted to the compact forward-invariant state space in which aspirations lie in the payoff interval. In the weak-selection regime, the first-order stationary abundance shift is positive when \(R+S>T+P\), negative when \(R+S T+P\) means that, under neutrality, the expected payoff of a cooperator exceeds that of a defector. The stationary variance reveals a different effect whose first-order correction is governed by the payoff-range contrast \((R-S)-(T-P)\). This contrast compares how strongly cooperator and defector payoffs respond to changes in local neighborhood composition and therefore measures the relative sensitivity of their payoffs to the local environment. Under degree-normalized average payoffs, these first-order results hold on every finite connected graph and are independent of degree sequence, topology, and aspiration learning rate. Simulations on regular and heterogeneous graphs compare averaged and accumulated payoffs and illustrate that graph heterogeneity and the aspiration learning rate can affect stationary behavior away from weak selection. The first-order coefficients are derived from the finite stochastic process and do not use pair approximation, mean-field closure, or a large-population limit.

items.title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. Here, we generate LLM-based political networks using personas sampled from the nationally representative ANES 2020--2022 Social Media Study and use respondents' survey-reported partisan exposure as an empirical benchmark for the political environments generated for the corresponding personas. We first characterize the structural properties and political assortativity of the generated networks, and then compare ego-level partisan exposure with the survey. We find that the structure and political assortativity of the generated networks vary across experimental configurations. More importantly, when comparing generated partisan exposure with the survey, some models generate stronger separation between Democratic and Republican egos than reported in the survey, with higher same-party and lower cross-party exposure, while others mainly underestimate Republican exposure across ego groups. Moreover, networks with similar political assortativity can still generate different partisan environments around the same personas, including among networks with plausible structural properties. Finally, generated networks show group-specific errors, under- or overestimating exposure to either Democrats or Republicans for specific social groups. These findings show that evaluating LLM-based social simulations only through aggregate outcomes can hide errors in the local environments through which those outcomes emerge, highlighting the importance of validation at both aggregate and individual levels.

items.title: Numerical study of multiple scattering intensities obtained from dust grains of different sizes and compositions in an impact-induced ejecta curtain
items.abstract: Impact cratering of celestial bodies produces an ejecta plume containing underground material, which helps us understand the properties of subsurface grains and the surface evolution. In most cases, the ejecta plume forms an inverted conical structure so-called ejecta curtain. In-situ measurements of light scattering of ejecta curtain, such as the images taken at the Hayabusa2's impact experiment help to constrain the size and composition of these less-processed grains using Monte-Carlo radiative transfer models. Here, we analyse the variation in the predicted scattered intensities of an ejecta curtain set up after that of Hayabusa2's case and test its sensitivity to different compositions, sizes, and phase function of grains. Initially, the optical depth of the ejecta curtain is assumed to be constant. The intensities are seen to deviate from single scattering expectations, which we attribute to the effect of varying scattering angles and optical depths of the photons. Further, we show the importance of using the phase function reproducing actual grain materials in place of HG phase function in impact plume modelling. The results are compared with different values of optical depth and the study is also extended to incorporate a grain-size distribution. It is observed that there is an increase in the magnitude of the model median scattered intensity with the decrease of the power index of the grain-size distribution. Nevertheless, the overall variation in the profile between the different compositions remained the same as that of the monodisperse case with uniform density across the ejecta cone. Thus, we envisage this study to serve as a useful reference for investigating the subsurface grain properties of planetary bodies via impact plume observations, and to aid in improving available ejecta scattering models and also in the selection of prospective targets for future impact missions.

items.title: Stochastic Shockwave Dynamics in First-Order Traffic Flow
items.abstract: Moving congestion fronts vary across realizations even when the traffic-flow law is fixed. This paper develops a generator-based formulation of the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) model with random initial density and a deterministic fundamental diagram. Randomness enters through the initial spatial density field; every realization follows the same conservation law. For a smooth strictly concave fundamental diagram, we adapt established one-sided spatial Markov closure to traffic variables under the stated spatial-process and regularity assumptions, and derive a kinetic balance for physically normalized front intensities. Evolving the spatial generator provides density laws and congestion-front statistics without solving a road-grid problem for every realization. The formulation is continuous in physical space and time, while its numerical implementation approximates density state and integrates physical time. Four experiments distinguish deterministic consistency from stochastic comparison. Riemann and signal examples recover independently constructed exact LWR solutions. Smooth strictly concave approximations approach the deterministic triangular-diagram signal solution over the tested finite horizons; this does not establish stochastic closure at contacts or the capacity kink. A matched Monte Carlo Godunov ensemble evaluates front counts, sizes, mergers, and density distributions. The evolved generator also yields an instantaneous travel-time distribution for a frozen density field, compared with the same functional of the matched Godunov profiles. This quantity is not experienced travel time through evolving traffic. Resolution checks identify remaining normalization and small-front-loss effects. The contribution is direct evolution and interpretation of traffic-state and front distributions under a fixed first-order traffic law.

items.title: A cross-sectional study of the prevalence and correlates of post-traumatic stress among people attending acceptance and commitment therapy for chronic pain.
items.abstract: Experiences of trauma are common among people with chronic pain, although estimates of comorbid post-traumatic stress vary widely across contexts. Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which targets psychological flexibility to improve pain-related functioning, is increasingly delivered for people with pain. To inform treatment delivery, understanding of the prevalence and correlates of post-traumatic stress among those attending ACT-based treatment for pain is needed. This study aimed to identify the prevalence of post-traumatic stress and its associations with key pain-related outcomes and other relevant psychosocial factors at the start of an ACT-based treatment. This was a cross-sectional study using data collected within routine clinical care at a speciality pain management service in the UK. Four hundred and fifty-one participants completed standardized self-report questionnaires of post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS), pain-related outcomes (pain intensity and interference, work and social adjustment, and depression symptoms), psychological flexibility/inflexibility, and stigma at the start of an interdisciplinary ACT-based treatment for chronic pain. Forty-seven percent of patients (n = 213) reported a traumatic exposure and 30% of the sample reported clinically meaningful PTSS. Greater severity of PTSS and probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were associated with significantly worse pain-related outcomes, psychological flexibility/inflexibility, and stigma in bivariate analyses. PTSS severity and probable PTSD showed significant unique associations with poorer pain outcomes in regression models controlling for covariates and psychological flexibility/inflexibility. Post-traumatic stress is common among people engaging in ACT-based treatment for pain and associated with adverse pain outcomes. Trauma-informed practice is therefore important when providing ACT-based treatment for pain.

items.title: Sexual dimorphism and body shape differences in hip bone morphology between Homo sapiens and Neanderthal lineage individuals.
items.abstract: The pelvis as a whole and the hip bones are the best skeletal elements for determining sex in humans, as their pattern of sexual dimorphism is based on women's ability to give birth to a full-term fetus. Additionally, an individual's body type also has a significant effect on pelvic shape, which could, in turn, influence the pattern of sexual dimorphism. It has been demonstrated that 3D geometric morphometrics (3DGM) can distinguish between male and female hip bone morphology in anatomically modern humans. Therefore, this study employs 3DGM methodology to analyse and compare hip bone morphology of individuals from the Neanderthal lineage, as well as a specimen of early Homo, in a comparative framework of 46 H. sapiens of known sex. The Neanderthal lineage individuals were distributed along modern male and female morphologies, coinciding with their traditional sexual assessment, based on differences in pubic length, iliac width, and greater sciatic notch aperture. These results point to a similar coxal sexual dimorphism pattern in both lineages. Body shape does not seem to influence the dimorphic pattern, but the results show a gradient from archaic coxal morphology present in early Homo to the derived Neanderthal morphology, where the pre- Neanderthal individual has a more Neanderthal-like morphology than the H. heidelbergensis individual.

items.title: A call for minimum standards in methodological reporting for studies using animal-borne accelerometers.
items.abstract: Animal-borne tri-axial accelerometers are increasingly used to investigate animal behaviour and energetics. Critical methodological details, such as device placement and dynamic range, are frequently underreported. This lack of reporting hampers study replicability and interpretation of results. It also complicates comparisons between studies. In addition, as device placement and attachment method can impact animal welfare and survival, transparent reporting should be considered vital for ethical publication. In this comment, we highlight these issues through a review of methodological reporting in studies involving attaching accelerometers to sea turtles. To address these challenges, we propose a framework for minimum standardised reporting that outlines key metadata which researchers should include when publishing studies utilizing animal-borne accelerometers. We also recommend thorough testing of devices and attachment methods prior to their use in the field. Adoption of this framework will enhance transparency, reproducibility, and comparability across studies, while promoting best practices in animal welfare. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40317-026-00506-9.

items.title: Optimizing Marine eDNA Protocols for Rare Megafauna: A Case Study on Dugongs in the Western Indian Ocean.
items.abstract: Assessing habitat use, spatial distribution, and site fidelity is critical for the conservation of threatened marine species, yet monitoring rare and elusive species in these types of complex environments remains difficult. This limitation is particularly critical for dugong (Dugong dugon) populations in the Western Indian Ocean, which are extremely small, fragmented, and difficult to monitor, posing a major conservation challenge. This pilot study aimed to develop a cost-effective and field-optimized eDNA workflow based on species-specific qPCR for large-scale monitoring of this threatened sirenian in shallow tropical coastal ecosystems. Field sampling was conducted in Mozambique, which hosts the only remaining large dugong population in the region. Using a species-specific qPCR assay independently developed and validated for this study, we evaluated how sampling design and sample processing influence dugong eDNA detection under natural conditions. Sampling was conducted along survey tracks using different sampling and DNA extraction strategies to evaluate three key variables of the detection protocol-(i) vertical sampling position (surface, near-bottom, and sediment), (ii) filtration volume (1.5, 30, and 60 L), and (iii) field versus laboratory DNA extraction-resulting in a total of 11 sampling-extraction strategies. At every visually confirmed location, at least one of the 11 sampling-extraction strategies resulted in a positive detection, including up to 2 h after the last visual sighting. All strategies detected dugong DNA except those based on sediment sampling. qPCR detection was influenced by an interaction between filtration volume and vertical sampling position: at low filtration volume (1.5 L), detection was higher near the bottom than at the surface, whereas this difference disappeared at 60 L. Conversely, increasing filtration volume improved detection at the surface but had little effect near the bottom. Laboratory extractions markedly outperformed field extractions. The sampling strategy yielding the highest detection rate-large-volume near-bottom filtration followed by laboratory-based sample processing-detected dugong DNA in all cases where a visual sighting had occurred. Overall, these results show that filtration volume can partly compensate for differences in detection associated with vertical sampling position and provide a robust and field-applicable framework for eDNA-based dugong monitoring, supporting scalable and long-term surveillance efforts in tropical coastal ecosystems.

items.title: Fungal Needle Communities and Dothistroma septosporum Occurrence in Pinus sylvestris Stands in Slovakia.
items.abstract: Dothistroma needle blight (DNB), caused by Dothistroma septosporum, is a globally important disease of pines, yet its ecological role within native host systems remains incompletely understood. We combined species-specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) with ITS2 metabarcoding to investigate the occurrence of D. septosporum and associated needle mycobiomes of Pinus sylvestris in natural stands in Slovakia with a pooled non-natural positive-reference group included for comparison. D. septosporum was detected in the Vernár natural stand (11 of 16 samples), where visible DNB symptoms were also observed, and in all samples of the non-natural positive-reference group (15 of 15 samples). The pathogen was not detected in the other three sampled natural stands. Fungal community analyzes revealed significant differences in community composition among sample groups, while alpha diversity patterns showed comparatively minor variation. The most abundant genus across all sites was Lophodermium, whereas Dothistroma was highly abundant only in the non-natural positive-reference group. Co-occurrence network analysis indicated that fungal communities were dominated by positive associations; however, patterns involving Dothistroma primarily reflected the positive-reference group, where the pathogen was highly abundant. Our results suggest that D. septosporum is not a consistently detectable component of needle mycobiomes in native P. sylvestris stands in Slovakia and that its high abundance in the non-natural positive-reference group was associated with a distinct fungal community composition.

items.title: Assessing the Potential Distribution of Eriocheir sinensis Under Climate Change: Regional Contrasts and Spatial Mismatches in Terrestrial and Nearshore Suitability.
items.abstract: The Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis), native to China and the Korean Peninsula, has established invasive populations with substantial ecological and economic impacts in Europe and North America. Anticipating changes in its potential distribution is important for invasion-risk screening and estuarine management. We developed a global species distribution model (G-SDM) and regional models for the native range, Europe, and North America, each comprising terrestrial and nearshore brackish-water components. Future suitability was projected under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585. Terrestrial PCA-env analyses assessed changes in projected suitable environmental space, whereas MESS and MoD diagnosed environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty. Terrestrial suitability was mainly associated with annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, and distance to the coastline, whereas nearshore suitability was mainly associated with water depth, chlorophyll concentration, and sea-surface temperature, although the ranking of predictor importance differed among regions. Predicted-suitable environments in Europe and North America extended to lower annual and wettest-quarter temperatures than those in the native range. Under future scenarios, projected suitability was generally redistributed towards higher latitudes, particularly under SSP585. Terrestrial suitability showed more pronounced spatial redistribution than nearshore suitability in several regions, and the two components were not always geographically aligned. Terrestrial PCA-env analyses indicated greater retention of suitable environmental space in Europe but increasing unfilling in the native range and North America. MESS analysis further identified environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty in some future suitable areas. These findings provide a scientific basis for early prevention, targeted monitoring, field validation, and estuarine management.

items.title: A validated amplicon panel for parentage reconstruction and selection monitoring in whitefish ( Coregonus spp.).
items.abstract: Fish populations are notoriously difficult to monitor because their aquatic habitats limit observation. While physical or chemical tagging (e.g., adipose fin removal or Alizarin Red S staining of bones) can reduce growth or survival or requires sacrifice, genetic tools offer a less invasive and more informative alternative, allowing managers to assess stock composition and census size while enabling researchers to study ecological and evolutionary processes. Here, we introduce a novel whitefish (Coregonus spp.) amplicon panel with 2,282 SNP loci identified using whole-genome resequencing, targeting loci spread across the whitefish genome, including candidate regions relevant to growth and immunity. We successfully applied the panel in seven whitefish species (C. cf. suidteri, C. confusus, C. albellus, C. muelleri, C. fatioi, C. palaea, and one C. sp.) from seven Swiss lakes. To evaluate performance, we used offspring of known parentage from an in vitro breeding experiment with wild-caught C. confusus. Parentage assignment on 381 families yielded a 0% error rate, even when parental genotypes were missing. This panel provides a robust tool for a wide range of applications in broad taxonomic and geographic contexts for monitoring whitefish populations, a group that has historically been difficult to study within the salmonid family. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12686-026-01449-2.

items.title: Wild Bee Conservation: Habitat Heterogeneity and Ecological Improvement in Agricultural Land With Open Grassland.
items.abstract: Wild bee populations are declining due to habitat loss and degradation. Flower-rich heterogenous grasslands have the potential to compensate for the loss and provide valuable habitat for wild bees. To investigate the effects of different levels of habitat heterogeneity and of ecological habitat improvement to increase foraging resources on wild bee communities, we comparatively studied two Central European grassland types in Austria (AT) and Luxembourg (LU) using pan traps. We collected and identified > 5000 individuals representing considerable fractions of wild bee fauna of these countries and characterised habitat heterogeneity (number of habitat elements, ecotone lengths) using GIS data and flower-colour abundance (white, yellow, blue) using drone imaging. Our findings suggest that macro-scale heterogeneity alone may not drive wild bee assemblages in LU, pointing to the potential overriding importance of unmeasured microhabitat variables, such as nesting substrates and taxonomic floral composition. In AT, however, wild bee abundance increased with habitat heterogeneity as measured by the length of ecotones with trees and bushes. Ecological improvement of habitat was important in LU, in that formerly intensively farmed land with sown wildflower fallows hosted higher richness and abundance than extensively used grassland. In AT, in contrast, higher species richness and abundance occurred in extensively used grassland than in formerly intensively farmed land with wildflower strips; here, overall increased floral resource abundance on ecologically improved sites seemed to have less influence, and flower species diversity, the quality of floral resources or any combination of flower properties, may have been more important than just its quantity as assessed by flower-colour abundance. In conclusion, we emphasise the relevance of regional habitat heterogeneity to wild bees and the opportunities by ecological improvement of intensively farmed land. Conservation strategies should be tailored to regional landscape contexts, prioritising extensive grassland protection in Austria and targeted wildflower fallow establishment in Luxembourg.

items.title: Single-Cell Detection and Quantification of Metabolically Active Bacteria in Soil Using Heavy-Water Labeling and Raman Microspectroscopy.
items.abstract: Only microorganisms that are metabolically active during a defined observation window contribute directly to ongoing soil processes, yet this active fraction is difficult to quantify. Cultivation excludes uncultured taxa, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)-based methods primarily describe community membership and functional potential, and bulk assays obscure cell-to-cell variation. This protocol combines heavy-water (D₂O) labeling with single-cell Raman microspectroscopy, here termed Raman-deuterium isotope probing (Raman-DIP), to detect and quantify bacterial anabolic activity during labeling in soil. Matched soil samples are incubated under identical conditions with H₂O or D₂O. Microbial cells are then recovered by Nycodenz density separation, deposited on aluminum-coated slides, and analyzed individually. Deuterium incorporation into newly synthesized biomass produces a carbon-deuterium (C-D) band at 2,040-2,300 cm⁻¹. A cell is classified as detectably active when its C-D ratio exceeds a threshold derived from the matched H₂O control, and the active-cell fraction is calculated for each biological replicate. The method retains soil-matrix effects during labeling, does not require cultivation or a fluorescent activity probe, and reveals physiological heterogeneity that is lost in community-averaged measurements. Because D₂O supplies an isotopic label rather than an exogenous organic substrate, it can label diverse anabolic processes while limiting selection for a particular carbon source. The workflow is therefore suited to standardized comparisons of bacterial activity across soils and environmental treatments. It reports anabolic incorporation during the labeling interval rather than overall viability; nonlabeled cells should not automatically be interpreted as dead.

items.title: Balancing Food, Heat and Predation Risk: Seasonal and Diel Movement Strategies of African Herbivores.
items.abstract: Understanding how large herbivores adjust their movement patterns in response to seasonal environmental variation is important for wildlife management. We investigated how sympatric African herbivores with contrasting body size, digestive systems and forage specialisation adjust their movement across seasons and the diel cycle. Using high-resolution GPS data from 16 plains zebra (Equus quagga; hindgut fermenter) and 8 tsessebe (Damaliscus lunatus; ruminant) between 2014 and 2016 in the Okavango Delta, Botswana, we quantified 24 h range size, 24 h displacement distance, as well as displacement distance and tortuosity across 4 h time blocks, and evaluated these movements in response to season, maximum daily air temperature and vegetation greenness. Zebra occupied 24 h ranges double that of tsessebe during the rainy and early flood seasons, but 24 h range size converged during the late flood season. Zebra travelled twice the distance of tsessebe over 24 h during the early flood season, whereas travelling distances were similar during the rainy and late flood seasons. At finer temporal scales, both species showed pronounced but seasonally variable diel movement patterns. Movement paths were generally less tortuous in zebra than tsessebe, although interspecific differences diminished during the late flood season and midday. Movement patterns also changed with environmental conditions: increasing maximum daily air temperature was associated with a stronger reduction in movement in zebra than in tsessebe, whereas increasing vegetation productivity was associated with larger 24 h ranges and increased tortuosity, with the latter response stronger in zebra. Overall, our findings demonstrate that movement differences between zebra and tsessebe are strongly context-dependent rather than constant across seasons. Movement convergence during the late flood season suggests that seasonal conditions can reduce otherwise pronounced interspecific differences in movement patterns. These findings improve our understanding of large herbivores' responses to seasonal environmental variation and may help predict species-specific responses to future climate change.

items.title: Linking Plant Community Characteristics and Soil Properties Under Grazing Disturbance in a Desert Steppe Ecosystem.
items.abstract: Grazing is a key driver of structural and functional changes in desert steppe ecosystems. Soil nutrients are essential for plant growth, and grazing can alter soil nutrient availability through herbivory and trampling, which, in turn, may affect plant communities. However, the responses of plant communities and their functional groups to soil properties under different grazing intensities remain elusive. This study examined variations in plant community characteristics, including biomass, quantitative traits, and species diversity, under a gradient of grazing intensities. Species were classified into functional groups, and their corresponding soil physicochemical properties were analyzed. The results showed that aboveground biomass was highest under no grazing and light grazing, and lowest under extreme grazing. Height and coverage of annual and biennial forbs and perennial grasses declined sharply with increasing grazing intensity. Species richness and diversity indices reached their minimum values under heavy grazing, while Simpson's dominance index peaked. Soil analysis revealed that available nitrogen and available phosphorus declined with increasing grazing intensity. Pearson correlation analysis revealed positive relationships between available nitrogen, available phosphorus, and plant α-diversity, biomass, and basic traits. Structural equation modeling further showed that grazing not only directly affected plant communities but also influenced them indirectly through reductions in soil available nitrogen and available phosphorus. In conclusion, regulating grazing intensity to maintain soil nutrient availability may be important for sustaining the stability and functioning of desert steppe ecosystems.

items.title: Integrative Taxonomy Does Not Support a Cosmopolitan Desmophyllum pertusum : Resurrecting D. californicum and Validating the Genus Desmophyllum .
items.abstract: Reef-building corals are key contributors in marine ecosystems, from warm, shallow reefs to cold, deep-water habitats worldwide. Desmophyllym pertusum (Linnaeus, 1758) is one of the most important habitat-forming cold-water corals and has long been considered a cosmopolitan species. Yet phylogenetic relationships within the genus, as well as its relatedness to the synonymized genus Lophelia (Milne Edwards & Haime, 1849), remain poorly understood and debated. Here, we use nuclear ultraconserved elements and exons, complete mitochondrial genomes, and single nucleotide polymorphism data to show that populations of D. pertusum in the eastern and central North Pacific Ocean are genetically differentiated from those in the western and eastern Atlantic Ocean. Our results support the previously proposed synonymy of genera Lophelia and Desmophyllum (Ehrenberg, 1834). Morphological features of specimens from the Pacific Ocean, particularly budding pattern and corallite size, match those of the previously synonymized D. californicum comb. nov., which we therefore reinstate. We also incorporated solitary Desmophyllum spp. lineages into phylogenomic analyses, including a multispecies coalescence model. Taken together, these integrative taxonomic results indicate the presence of multiple Desmophyllum species beyond those currently recognized as valid. Future studies could incorporate phylogenomic approaches to better delimit species boundaries and avoid grouping distinct coral species.

items.title: Varroa-Sensitive Hygiene (VSH) as a Potential Contributor to the Natural Survival of Ethiopian Honey Bees ( Apis mellifera simensis ) Against Varroa destructor Mite.
items.abstract: Although the Varroa destructor mite is the primary threat to honey bee (Apis mellifera), populations of A. m. simensis in Ethiopia naturally survive mite infestations without treatment. While general hygienic and grooming behaviors have been previously reported to contribute to the natural survival of this subspecies against Varroa mites, the role of Varroa-sensitive hygiene (VSH) remains unknown. Here, we experimentally evaluated four VSH responses in worker brood cells of this subspecies artificially infested with a single mite (treatment) or opened and resealed without introducing a mite (control) across varying infested patch sizes (five, eight, and ten neighboring cells): untouched cells (UC), cell cap opened or partially opened (CO), brood and introduced mite removed (BMR), and introduced mite removed, brood retained, and cell recapped (MR). Our results revealed that VSH responses differed significantly between treatment categories and were significantly dependent on infested patch size. At five-cell patch size, VSH responses did not differ between treatment categories, whereas eight- and ten-cell patch sizes significantly increased the odds of BMR, MR and/or CO relative to UC by between five- and twenty-nine-fold. Model-predicted probabilities showed that the removal response (BMR + MR) accounted for 64.9% and 83.7% in infested patches at eight and ten cells, respectively, compared with 21.5% and 23.1% in controls. The uncapping response (CO + BMR + MR) reached 71.2% and 89.8% in eight and ten cells compared with 33.1% and 30.2% in controls, respectively. Overall, these findings suggest VSH as an additional behavioral mechanism of Ethiopian honey bees against V. destructor.

items.title: The illusion of conformity: when independent learning mimics social influence.
items.abstract: Although individuals tested in isolation often show substantial behavioral variation, they tend to behave more uniformly in groups, a pattern commonly attributed to social conformity (ie, a form of social learning in which individuals preferentially adopt the most common trait). However, evidence for social conformity in nonhuman animals remains debated, as group-level convergence can also arise from independent learning, where individuals adopt the trait maximizing their fitness. Such learning can generate either adaptive phenotypic convergence or pseudo-conformity when aligning with the group's average strategy provides a selective advantage (eg, by reducing predation risk). The likelihood of these outcomes is shaped by ecological and social factors, yet their relative contributions remain poorly understood, as most studies rely on simplified laboratory conditions. This study explores the conditions under which conformist-like patterns can emerge solely from individual learning, and how costs of deviating from the group strategy and tradeoffs between different selective pressures influence their evolution. I developed an evolutionary model in which individuals sequentially adjust their exploratory behavior through a trial-and-error learning process. At each learning step, an individual explores 2 small behavioral deviations around its current exploration level and retains the variant that yields the highest payoff under the prevailing ecological conditions. The results show that the likelihood of pseudo-conformity depends on the interplay among ecological conditions, group composition and behavioral flexibility, and is particularly favored when predation risk and the energetic costs of escaping predator attacks are high. Moreover, under some conditions, pseudo-conformity may maintain behavioral diversity at the population level by allowing different subgroups to converge on and stabilize around distinct behavioral phenotypes. Overall, these findings underscore that measuring traits in isolation may misrepresent both behavioral variation and evolutionary dynamics.

items.title: Combined Effects of Beetle Density and Sex Ratio on Reproductive Trade-Offs and Dung Burial in Tunnelling Dung Beetles.
items.abstract: Dung beetle density and sex ratio play a significant role in intraspecific competition, and reproductive success depends on the beetle's maturity. We examined the impact of increasing density in small groups on dung burial and brood production using mature first-generation individuals of two dung beetle species (Onthophagus binodis and Digitonthophagus gazella) by manipulating the number of males and females in a dung pat. Beetles were reared under controlled laboratory conditions and provided with cattle dung, which was collected from pastureland. Weekly dung burial was calculated by measuring the residual dung organic matter content. The number of broods produced per dung pat, broods' dry weight, and their size were recorded. In both species, treatments with intermediate numbers of male and female beetles produced more broods than solitary beetles. On the other hand, treatments with moderate to high numbers of male and female beetles buried more dung than individual females. At higher-density treatments, brood size and brood dry weight declined, suggesting shifts in reproductive allocation under increasing intraspecific interactions. The two species showed very similar patterns, although O. binodis produced more broods while D. gazella buried more dung. We also observed a positive relationship between brood dry weight and brood size in both species. Overall, the results indicate that the combined effects of beetle density and sex ratio influenced reproductive investment and dung burial under controlled laboratory conditions. Further field studies are needed to determine whether similar patterns occur under higher density and natural ecological conditions.
